items.caption: x = 3: true at one input, false everywhere else
items.text: The left side x is drawn as a curve and the right side 3 as a level; the equation asserts that they are equal, and that happens at exactly one input, where the curve crosses the level. At every other x the two sides differ, so the statement is false there. Move the marble along the axis and try other equations on the

items.caption: x² + 4 = 0: the empty solution set
items.text: The curve x² + 4 never comes down to the level 0, so no real input makes the two sides equal: the solution set over ℝ is empty, just as for the section's x² = −1. Lower the curve until it touches or crosses the level, and the set gains one or two members, as x² = 4 has {−2, 2}. Try it on the

items.caption: 3x − 2 = 4: one crossing
items.text: The line y = 3x − 2 meets the level y = 4 exactly once, at x = 2, and the marker sits on that crossing: a linear equation has one solution because a non-horizontal line crosses any level exactly once. Change the slope or the level and the single crossing simply moves. Drag the level line on the

items.caption: x² − 4 = 0: two crossings
items.text: The parabola meets the axis at x = −2 and x = 2, so the equation has two real solutions; raise the level above the vertex and the crossings vanish, set it on the vertex and they merge into one. The number of solutions is the number of times the curve meets the line, which is what the discriminant counts. Slide the level through the vertex on the

items.caption: x³ − 3x = 0: three crossings
items.text: The cubic crosses the axis three times, at −√3, 0 and √3, the maximum a degree-three equation allows; shift the level up and one crossing at a time disappears until a single one remains, never none, because a cubic always crosses every level. Degree bounds the count, shape decides it. Move the level and count the marbles on the

items.caption: Excluded values first, solutions second
items.text: The section's equation 3/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 4) = 1. Its left side is undefined at x = 1 and x = −4, where the graph breaks at the dashed lines; those inputs are ruled out before solving. Clearing denominators gives x² − 2x − 14 = 0, so x = 1 ± √15, and neither is an excluded value: both are the points where the curve meets y = 1.

items.caption: |x| = 3: the V crosses the level twice
items.text: The V-shaped graph of |x| meets the level y = 3 at x = −3 and x = 3: the two cases of the case-splitting method are the two arms of the V. Lower the level to 0 and the crossings merge at the corner; lower it further and there are none. Watch the two solutions appear and disappear on the

items.caption: |x| + 5 = 2: no solution
items.text: The V-shaped curve |x| + 5 never drops below 5, so it never reaches the level 2: the equation, which says |x| = −3, asks a distance to be negative and has no solution. Checking the sign of the right-hand side settles this before any case split. Slide the level and watch solutions appear on the

items.caption: |x| = 3 has solutions x = −3 and x = 3
items.text: The level y = 3 cuts both arms of the V, so B > 0 gives two solutions; at B = 0 the level touches only the corner and there is one; below the axis the level misses the graph and there is none. The three structures of the section are three positions of one line. Slide the level through the three cases on the

items.secTitle: Solving Equations of the Form |f(x)| = k
items.caption: Two cases, one of them empty
items.text: The section's |x² − 4| = 5. The bars fold the dipping part of x² − 4 (dashed) up above the axis. The case x² − 4 = 5 meets the level at x = ±3; the case x² − 4 = −5 would need the dashed parabola to reach −5, which it never does, so it adds nothing. The solution set is {−3, 3}.

items.secTitle: Equations with Absolute Value on Both Sides
items.caption: Two V-shapes, two crossings
items.text: The section's |2x − 1| = |x + 4|, each side drawn as its own V. They meet where the magnitudes agree: at x = 5 the insides are equal (9 and 9), and at x = −1 they are opposites (−3 and 3). These are exactly the two cases f(x) = g(x) and f(x) = −g(x).

items.caption: Where squaring goes wrong
items.text: The section's |x − 2| = 3x − 4. The V and the line meet once, at x = 3/2. Squaring both sides also produces x = 1, but on the dashed line x = 1 the two sides are 1 and −1: equal in square, not in value. Because the right side is negative there, x = 1 is extraneous.

items.caption: −x + 5 = 0: the line crosses the axis at x = 5
items.text: The standard form ax + b = 0 asks where the line y = ax + b meets the x-axis, and for −x + 5 that is x = 5, the single marked crossing. The condition a ≠ 0 is what keeps the line from being horizontal, which is what guarantees the crossing exists. Tilt the line by changing a on the

items.caption: 2 = 3: a horizontal line that never reaches the level
items.text: When the variable cancels the left side is a constant, a horizontal line, and either it coincides with the level line, every x a solution, or, as here with 2 = 3, it runs parallel below it and there is no solution at all. No crossing, no marble. Compare the two degenerate cases on the

items.caption: x³ − 3x = 0: degree 3, three real roots
items.text: The degree of the equation is the highest power present, and it caps the number of crossings with the level line: this cubic reaches its cap of three. A quadratic could show at most two, a linear equation exactly one. Raise the degree and count how many crossings become possible on the

items.caption: Degree 4, four roots, two conjugate pairs
items.text: z⁴ + 1 = 0 has real coefficients but no real root, since z⁴ is never negative for real z. In ℂ it has exactly four roots, one per degree, as the theorem promises. They sit in mirror pairs across the real axis, (1 + i)/√2 with (1 − i)/√2 and (−1 + i)/√2 with (−1 − i)/√2: each pair multiplies out to a real quadratic factor, here x² − √2x + 1 and x² + √2x + 1.

items.caption: Candidates versus roots
items.text: The section's cubic 2x³ − 3x² − 8x + 12. The theorem lists sixteen possible rational roots; the graph crosses the axis at only three of them, −2, 3/2 and 2. Testing the list by substitution finds x = 2 first; dividing out (x − 2) leaves 2x² + x − 6 = (2x − 3)(x + 2), which gives the other two.

items.caption: Four, two or no real roots
items.text: Three bi-quadratics, each solved by u = x². x⁴ − 5x² + 4 gives u = 1 or 4, so x = ±1, ±2: four real roots. x⁴ − 2x² − 3 gives u = 3 or −1, and only u = 3 yields real x = ±√3: two real roots. x⁴ + 1 never reaches 0: no real roots at all, unlike a cubic, which always crosses the axis at least once.

items.caption: x³ = 0: one root of multiplicity three
items.text: The curve flattens against the axis at the origin and passes through without the usual crossing angle: the root x = 0 appears three times in the factorisation x · x · x, and the flattening is what a triple root looks like. A double root would touch and turn back instead. Compare the touch of x² = 0 with this crossing on the

items.caption: x² − 2x − 3 = 5: a quadratic not yet in standard form
items.text: The left side is drawn as a parabola and the right side 5 as a level above the axis; the solutions are where the two meet. Moving the 5 across gives x² − 2x − 8 = 0, which lowers the parabola by 5 so the same solutions become its crossings of the axis, the standard-form picture. Shift the level yourself on the

items.caption: Factoring turns one quadratic into two linear equations
items.text: The section's x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3). The two factor lines cross the axis at x = 2 and x = 3, and the parabola, their product, is zero at exactly those inputs and nowhere else: a product vanishes only when one of its factors does.

items.caption: x² + 6x + 5 = 0 becomes (x + 3)² − 4 = 0
items.text: The x² block and the 6x strip, split into two 3x halves, form an incomplete square; adding the 3 × 3 corner completes it, and the constant 5 falls short of that 9 by 4, so the equation reads (x + 3)² = 4 and x + 3 = ±2. items.caption: x² + 4 = 0: the parabola never reaches the axis
items.text: The vertex sits at height 4 above the axis, so no real x makes the expression zero: the discriminant 0² − 4 · 1 · 4 = −16 is negative and there are no crossings to mark. Lower the parabola by 4 and the crossings merge into one at the vertex; lower it further and two appear. Watch the discriminant change sign on the

items.caption: x² − 4 = 0: the solutions are the x-intercepts
items.text: The two crossings of the parabola with the axis, at −2 and 2, are the two solutions of the equation: solving a quadratic and finding the x-intercepts of its graph are the same task. The vertex halfway between them sits on the axis of symmetry x = −b/2a. Drag the parabola and watch the intercepts move together on the

items.caption: The excluded value is a wall, not a solution
items.text: The section's x/(x − 3) = 9/(x − 3) + 2, each side drawn as its own graph. Both break at the dashed line x = 3, where the shared denominator is zero: no point of either graph exists there, so 3 is declared out of the domain before solving. The graphs meet once, at x = −3, where both sides equal 1/2.

items.caption: An identity with one point missing
items.text: The section's x/(x − 3) − 3/(x − 3) = 1. The left side simplifies to (x − 3)/(x − 3), which is 1 wherever it is defined, so its graph lies exactly on the right side y = 1, except for the open circle at x = 3, where it is undefined. Clearing denominators reports 0 = 0; the graph shows the solution set is every real number except 3.

items.caption: A candidate that lands on an excluded value
items.text: The section's 2/(x² − 1) = 1/(x − 1). Clearing denominators gives 2 = x + 1, so x = 1, but x = 1 is one of the excluded values (dashed). The graphs confirm it: the two sides never meet anywhere in the domain, and the only place the algebra points to is the vertical line where both are undefined. The equation has no solution.

items.text: A square of side a + b + c, cut along a, b and c in both directions, falls into nine rectangles: three squares a², b², c² on the diagonal and six off-diagonal pieces, each product ab, ac, bc appearing twice, once on each side of the diagonal. items.caption: (x + 2)(x − 1)(x − 5) < 0: two stretches of the line
items.text: The curve dips below the axis twice, and every input in those stretches makes the expression negative: the solution set is not a list of values but the blue bars on the axis, everything left of −2 and everything between 1 and 5. The open circles mark boundaries that do not satisfy the strict inequality. Try other expressions on the

items.caption: The same expression with ≤: the boundaries join the set
items.text: Changing < to ≤ keeps the same stretches but fills in the circles at −2, 1 and 5, because the expression equals 0 there and 0 ≤ 0 is true. In interval notation the parentheses become brackets: (−∞, −2] ∪ [1, 5]. The infinite end keeps its parenthesis, since ∞ is never a number to include. Switch operators on the

items.caption: (x + 2)(x − 1)(x − 5) < 0: the sign chart
items.text: The three roots cut the axis into four intervals and the chart records the sign of the product on each: negative, positive, negative, positive from left to right. The inequality holds exactly on the shaded intervals where the curve is below the axis. Change an operator or a root and watch the shading redistribute on the

items.caption: Why dividing by a negative flips the sign
items.text: The section's −3x ≥ 12. The line y = −3x falls as x grows, so it sits on or above the level 12 only for x at or left of −4. Dividing both sides by −3 must therefore turn ≥ into ≤: the answer is x ≤ −4, not x ≥ −4.

items.caption: (x + 2)(x − 3) < 0: between the roots
items.text: The parabola dips below the axis only between its two roots, so the solution is the single interval (−2, 3); with a negative discriminant the parabola would never dip and the solution would be empty or everything. The roots are the boundaries, the leading coefficient the orientation. Flip the sign of the leading coefficient on the

items.caption: (x + 3)(x − 2)² < 0: a double root does not change the sign
items.text: At x = 2 the curve touches the axis and turns back without crossing, so the sign is the same on both sides of that root, while at the simple root x = −3 it crosses and the sign flips. The solution is the interval left of −3 alone. Watch which roots flip the chart on the

items.caption: (x − 1)/(x + 2) < 0: two kinds of critical point
items.text: The numerator zero at x = 1 and the pole at x = −2 both cut the axis, and the expression is negative only between them; the pole is drawn as an asymptote and can never belong to the solution, while the numerator zero joins it only for a non-strict inequality. Toggle strictness and watch the endpoints open and close on the

items.caption: |x| − 3 < 0: the V dips below the axis on (−3, 3)
items.text: The V-shaped graph is below the axis exactly between its two zeros, so the less-than form gives one bounded interval; the greater-than form would give the two outer rays instead. That is the compound inequality −3 < x < 3 as a picture. Switch the operator on the

items.caption: One interval or two rays
items.text: With k = 3: |x| < 3 asks for points within 3 of zero, a single bounded interval from −3 to 3, written as the conjunction −3 < x < 3. |x| > 3 asks for points more than 3 from zero, two rays heading away from each other, written as the disjunction x < −3 or x > 3. Both boundaries are open because both inequalities are strict.

items.secTitle: Absolute Value Inequalities with Quadratic or Other Expressions
items.caption: Three pieces from one inequality
items.text: The section's |x² − 7x + 10| ≥ 2. The bars fold the dip of the parabola between 2 and 5 upward, and the folded hump just reaches above 2 between x = 3 and x = 4. Together with the two outer arms, the graph is on or above the level on three pieces: x ≤ (7 − √17)/2 ≈ 1.44, 3 ≤ x ≤ 4, and x ≥ (7 + √17)/2 ≈ 5.56.

items.caption: Where the boundary comes from
items.text: The section's 4x − 7 ≤ 2x + 11, with each side drawn as a line. They cross at x = 9, the solution of the equation 4x − 7 = 2x + 11: that is the boundary point. To the left of 9 the steeper line 4x − 7 is below the other, so the inequality holds there; the crossing itself counts because the inequality is non-strict. The solution is (−∞, 9].

items.caption: AND versus OR on the number line
items.text: The section's two compound inequalities. The chain −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 needs both parts at once, which leaves the overlap −2 < x ≤ 3: open at −2, closed at 3. The disjunction x + 3 < −1 or x + 3 > 5 needs only one part, which leaves two separate rays, x < −4 and x > 2, with the gap between them excluded.

items.text: With roots at −2, 1 and 5 the axis splits into four intervals, and because each root is simple the sign flips at every one of them: the chart reads −, +, −, + and the strict inequality selects the two shaded intervals. items.caption: The double root at x = 2 keeps the sign
items.text: The factor (x − 2)² is never negative, so the curve touches the axis at 2 and bounces back: the sign chart shows the same sign on both sides of that root, and only the simple root at −3 produces a flip. items.secTitle: Polynomials That Do Not Factor Over the Rationals
items.caption: A boundary that is not a rational number
items.text: The section's x³ − 2 > 0. Its only real root is ∛2 ≈ 1.26, which the rational root theorem could never find, yet it splits the line exactly like any other root: the curve is below the axis to its left and above it to its right. The solution is (∛2, ∞), with the boundary excluded because the inequality is strict.

items.caption: Reading the signs from the ends inward
items.text: The section's (x + 2)²(x − 1)(x − 4) > 0. Its leading term x⁴ makes both ends positive. Moving inward from the right, the simple root 4 flips the sign to negative and the simple root 1 flips it back to positive; the double root −2 only touches the axis, so the sign stays positive on both sides. Excluding the roots themselves, the solution is x < −2, −2 < x < 1, or x > 4.

items.caption: Before and after standard form
items.text: The section's x² < 3x + 10, with each side drawn as its own graph. The parabola dips below the line between their crossings at x = −2 and x = 5, so that stretch is the solution. Moving everything to one side gives x² − 3x − 10 < 0, whose roots are the same −2 and 5: rewriting in standard form changes how the question looks, not its answer.

items.secTitle: Solving When the Discriminant Is Positive
items.caption: Δ > 0: the parabola dips between its two roots
items.text: With two roots the parabola crosses the axis twice and lies below it exactly between the crossings, so ax² + bx + c < 0 holds on (−2, 3) and the reverse inequality holds on the two outer rays. The leading coefficient decides which of the two patterns applies. Flip a and watch the shading invert on the

items.secTitle: Solving When the Discriminant Is Zero
items.caption: A single root that never changes the sign
items.text: With Δ = 0 the quadratic is a perfect square, here (x − 2)². It touches the axis at x = 2 and is positive everywhere else. So (x − 2)² > 0 holds for every x except 2 (the open circle), ≥ 0 holds for every real number, < 0 never holds, and ≤ 0 holds only at x = 2.

items.secTitle: Solving When the Discriminant Is Negative
items.caption: Δ < 0: x² + 4 never reaches the axis
items.text: The parabola floats above the axis, never touching it, so x² + 4 is positive for every real x: the inequality x² + 4 < 0 has no solution at all, and x² + 4 > 0 has every real number. With no roots there are no boundaries and the sign is constant. See the empty solution set on the

items.caption: A quartic inequality solved as a quadratic
items.text: The section's x⁴ − 5x² + 4 > 0. With u = x² it becomes (u − 1)(u − 4) > 0, true for u < 1 or u > 4. Back in x, u < 1 is −1 < x < 1 and u > 4 is x < −2 or x > 2: exactly the three stretches where the curve is above the axis, with the four boundaries ±1 and ±2 excluded.

items.page: Rational Inequalities: Sign Charts & Critical Points
items.caption: Numerator zero at 1, pole at −2
items.text: Both critical points divide the axis, but they behave differently: at x = 1 the expression is zero and the curve crosses the axis, while at x = −2 the denominator vanishes and the curve runs off along the dashed asymptote. The solution, the interval between them, can include the first endpoint but never the second. Distinguish the two kinds on the

items.page: Rational Inequalities: Sign Charts & Critical Points
items.caption: What cross-multiplying gets wrong
items.text: The section's (x − 3)/(x + 2) > 1. Multiplying by x + 2 as if it were positive gives −3 > 2, which suggests no solution. The graph disagrees: left of the wall at x = −2 the whole branch lies above y = 1, because there x + 2 is negative and the multiplication should have flipped the inequality. Rewriting as −5/(x + 2) > 0 gives the true answer, x < −2.

items.page: Rational Inequalities: Sign Charts & Critical Points
items.caption: Two kinds of critical points on one graph
items.text: The section's (7 − x)/((x − 3)(x + 1)) ≤ 0. The denominator zeros −1 and 3 are walls where the graph breaks and the expression is undefined, so they are excluded even though the inequality is non-strict. The numerator zero 7 is where the graph touches 0, so it is included. The graph is on or below the axis on −1 < x < 3 and from 7 onward, where it stays just below the axis.

items.caption: Two points every logarithm shares
items.text: log₂ x, ln x and log₁₀ x drawn together. All three cross the axis at x = 1, because a⁰ = 1 for every base, so log_a(1) = 0. Each also reaches height 1 exactly at its own base, (2, 1), (e, 1) and (10, 1), because a¹ = a. The larger the base, the further right that second anchor sits and the flatter the curve.

items.caption: The logarithm undoes the exponential
items.text: 2ˣ and log₂ x are mirror images in the dashed line y = x. The point (2, 4) on 2ˣ says 2² = 4; its mirror (4, 2) on log₂ x says log₂(4) = 2. Following one graph and then the other returns to the start, which is what the identities log_a(aˣ) = x and a^(log_a x) = x state in symbols.

items.page: Common & Natural Logarithms: Log vs Ln Explained
items.caption: One curve, two vertical scales
items.text: ln x and log x drawn together. Both cross the axis at (1, 0). The natural logarithm reaches 1 already at x = e ≈ 2.718, the common logarithm only at x = 10, so ln x is the steeper of the two. At x = 10 the dashed line shows the fixed ratio between them: log 10 = 1 while ln 10 ≈ 2.303, and the same factor 2.303 links their heights at every x.

items.caption: Why x = −2 is thrown out
items.text: The section's log₂ x + log₂(x − 2) = 3. The left side only exists for x > 2, where both arguments are positive, so its graph starts at the dashed line. It meets the level 3 once, at x = 4. Condensing to x² − 2x = 8 also produces x = −2, but no part of the graph lives there: log₂(−2) is undefined, so the candidate is rejected.

items.caption: A quadratic hiding inside a logarithm
items.text: The section's (log₂ x)² − 5 log₂ x + 6 = 0. In terms of u = log₂ x it is u² − 5u + 6 = 0, with u = 2 or u = 3, so x = 4 or x = 8. The graph confirms both: it reaches zero exactly there, dipping slightly below the axis between them.

items.caption: Two exponentials with different bases
items.text: The section's 2ˣ⁺³ = 5ˣ⁻¹. The left side starts higher, but base 5 grows faster, so the two curves cross exactly once. Taking logarithms of both sides brings the exponents down and gives x = (ln 5 + 3 ln 2)/(ln 5 − ln 2) ≈ 4.026, the crossing in the graph.

items.caption: Equal steps from doubling
items.text: log₂ x passes through (1, 0), (2, 1), (4, 2) and (8, 3): every time x doubles, the output goes up by exactly 1. That is why the curve keeps rising forever yet flattens out: reaching the next unit of height takes twice as long a stretch of x as the last one.

items.text: Near x = 0 both curves run along the y-axis without touching it. log₂ x plunges toward −∞ and log₁⁄₂ x climbs toward +∞, but neither ever reaches x = 0, where no power of the base gives 0. Away from the axis the two are mirror images across the x-axis.

items.caption: Lifting the curve
items.text: The section's log₃ x + 2 against log₃ x. Every point rises 2 units: (1, 0) becomes (1, 2) and (3, 1) becomes (3, 3). The asymptote is a vertical line, so a vertical shift leaves it at x = 0, and the domain is still x > 0.

items.caption: A vertical stretch by 2
items.text: The section's 2 log₂ x against log₂ x. Every output is doubled, so (2, 1) becomes (2, 2) and the curve is steeper everywhere. The point (1, 0) cannot move, because doubling 0 still gives 0, and the asymptote stays at x = 0.

items.caption: Two different reflections
items.text: The section's −log₂ x and log₂(−x) against log₂ x (dashed). Negating the output flips the curve across the x-axis: (2, 1) becomes (2, −1) and the function now decreases. Negating the input flips it across the y-axis: (2, 1) becomes (−2, 1) and the domain becomes x < 0.

items.page: Logarithmic Inequalities: Solving by Base Type
items.caption: The domain closes the interval
items.text: The section's log₄(x + 2) < 0. The algebra gives x + 2 < 1, so x < −1, a ray running off to the left. But the graph starts at the dashed line x = −2, where the argument reaches 0, and nothing exists to its left. The curve is below the axis only between that wall and x = −1: the solution is −2 < x < −1.

items.page: Logarithmic Inequalities: Solving by Base Type
items.caption: Bounding a logarithm on both sides
items.text: The section's 1 < log₂ x < 4. The curve sits between the two dashed levels exactly while x runs from 2 to 16: it crosses y = 1 at x = 2¹ = 2 and y = 4 at x = 2⁴ = 16. Because base 2 is greater than 1, both bounds keep their direction when converted.

items.page: Logarithmic Inequalities: Solving by Base Type
items.caption: Why the base decides the direction
items.text: log₂ x and log₁⁄₂ x against the same level y = 1. The rising curve log₂ x is above the level to the right of its crossing, so log₂ x > 1 means x > 2. The falling curve log₁⁄₂ x is above the level to the left of its crossing, so log₁⁄₂ x > 1 means 0 < x < 1/2. The same inequality has its answer on opposite sides.

items.page: Properties of Logarithms: Domain, Range & More
items.caption: The argument sets the domain
items.text: The section's two composite logarithms. log₂(x − 3) needs x − 3 > 0, so its graph begins at the dashed line x = 3 and nothing exists to the left. log₅(x² + 1) has an argument that is positive for every real x, so its graph runs across the whole axis, touching its lowest value 0 at x = 0.

items.page: Properties of Logarithms: Domain, Range & More
items.caption: One-to-one, seen with horizontal lines
items.text: Every horizontal line meets log₂ x exactly once, because the curve only ever rises: no two inputs share an output, so log₂(M) = log₂(N) forces M = N. The function log₂(x² + 1) is a different story: its argument falls and then rises again, so the graph turns back at 0 and the line y = 1 meets it at x = ±1. Two inputs share an output, and the one-to-one property fails.

items.caption: The product rule on the graph
items.text: The section's example on the curve y = log₂ x. At x = 4 the height is 2 and at x = 8 it is 3. Multiplying the inputs, 8 × 4 = 32, gives the point (32, 5), and 5 is exactly 3 + 2. The logarithm turns the multiplication of inputs into the addition of heights, which is the product rule log₂(xy) = log₂ x + log₂ y.

items.caption: x³ − 3x = x(x − √3)(x + √3): three roots, three crossings
items.text: Each linear factor contributes one crossing of the axis: at 0, at √3 and at −√3 the product vanishes because one factor does. Root and factor are the same information: r is a root exactly when (x − r) divides the polynomial, and the picture shows all three at once. Read the roots off the marbles on the

items.page: Roots of a Polynomial: Find Zeros & Solve Equations
items.caption: x³ = 0: the root 0 appears three times
items.text: The three factors are all x, so the single root has multiplicity three and the curve flattens as it passes through the origin; a double root would touch and turn back without crossing. Multiplicity is visible as the shape of the curve at the root. Compare x² = 0 and x³ = 0 on the

items.page: Roots of a Polynomial: Find Zeros & Solve Equations
items.caption: x² − 4 = 0: the real roots are the x-intercepts
items.text: The parabola crosses the axis at −2 and 2, the two real roots; complex roots, which the graph cannot show, would appear as a parabola that never reaches the axis. items.caption: x = 3, frozen
items.text: The identity line against level 3: one crossing, marked at x = 3. The marble waits at 0, its amber bar measuring the gap of 3 still to close.

items.caption: 3x − 2 = 4, frozen
items.text: Slope 3 makes the line race through the level at x = 2. Steepness changes the sensitivity of the solution, never the count.

items.caption: −x + 5 = 0, frozen
items.text: The downhill line: still one crossing, at x = 5, but the sign chart flips — positive left, negative right.

items.caption: 2 = 3 (a = 0), frozen
items.text: The degenerate line: slope zero, two parallel horizontals, no crossing anywhere. Zero solutions — or infinitely many if b = n.

items.caption: x² − 4 = 0, frozen
items.text: The generic parabola picture: two symmetric crossings at ±2, dashed drop-lines marking both. Positive discriminant, drawn.

items.caption: x² = 0, frozen
items.text: Tangency: the level grazes the vertex, one repeated root at 0 — and the marble happens to sit on it. Touch without crossing.

items.caption: x² + 4 = 0, frozen
items.text: The parabola floats above the level with nothing to mark. The picture of a negative discriminant — the roots have left the real line.

items.caption: x² − 2x − 3 = 5, frozen
items.text: Off-center crossings at −2 and 4: the level absorbed into the constant term, the symmetry axis shifted to x = 1.

items.caption: x³ − 3x = 0, frozen
items.text: The full S: hill and valley straddling the level, three crossings at −1.73, 0, 1.73. The cubic’s maximum count.

items.caption: x³ = 0, frozen
items.text: The monotone cube crosses every level exactly once — here at its flattened triple root through the origin.

items.caption: x³ − 4x = 3, frozen
items.text: The raised level still threads between hill and valley: three crossings, one exact (−1) and two irrational.

items.caption: |x| = 3, frozen
items.text: The V cut across both arms: two symmetric solutions at ±3 — two linear equations wearing one symbol.

items.caption: |x| + 3 = 3, frozen
items.text: Vertex meets level: a single touching point at x = 0, with a kink where the parabola would have a smooth turn.

items.caption: |x| + 5 = 2, frozen
items.text: The V floats three units above the level it can never reach: a distance asked to be negative. Empty, with no complex rescue.

items.caption: Operator <, frozen
items.text: The reference frame: negative intervals shaded, every boundary dot open — zero is not less than zero.

items.caption: Operator ≤, frozen
items.text: Same bars, filled dots: non-strict comparison admits the roots themselves, and nothing else changes.

items.caption: Operator >, frozen
items.text: Direction flipped: the complementary intervals light up, boundaries open again.

items.caption: Operator ≥, frozen
items.text: The fourth corner of the two-by-two: positive intervals with their endpoints included.

items.caption: (x+2)(x−1)(x−5) < 0, frozen
items.text: Four intervals, alternating signs, two shaded: the default state of the tool, with the marble certifying the leftmost interval from x = −4.

items.caption: (x+3)(x−2)² < 0, frozen
items.text: The squared factor cancels one sign change: the curve touches zero at 2 and bounces. Only the far-left interval survives.

items.caption: (x+1)(x)(x−1) < 0, frozen
items.text: Three roots in three units: rapid alternation, narrow intervals — x³ − x asked a different question.

items.caption: x² − x − 6 < 0, frozen
items.text: An upward parabola is negative between its roots: one connected bar from −2 to 3.

items.secTitle: A Quadratic with No Real Roots
items.caption: x² + 4 < 0, frozen
items.text: No roots, one sign, empty answer: the irreducible quadratic as an all-or-nothing gate.

items.caption: −x² + 2x + 3 < 0, frozen
items.text: Opens down, so “below zero” means outside the roots: the two outer rays are shaded, not the middle.

items.caption: |x| − 3 < 0, frozen
items.text: Distance under 3 from the origin: the valley of the V, shaded from −3 to 3.

items.caption: |x − 2| − 4 < 0, frozen
items.text: Center 2, radius 4, straight from the formula: the shaded interval runs −2 to 6.

items.caption: |x + 1| < 0, frozen
items.text: A distance asked to be negative: the vertex touches zero at −1 and nothing is shaded anywhere.

items.caption: (x−1)/(x+2) < 0, frozen
items.text: Blue zero, red pole, and the negative stretch between them. The red stripe marks the domain hole at −2.

items.caption: (x+3)/(x−4) < 0, frozen
items.text: Zero left, pole right, seven units of solution between — and the curve diving toward the asymptote at 4.

items.caption: (x−2)/(x−3) < 0, frozen
items.text: One unit between zero and pole: the entire solution squeezed into (2, 3).

items.caption: √x − 2 < 0, frozen
items.text: Red nothing left of 0, then a slow climb to the zero at 4. The solution lives between domain edge and crossing.

items.caption: √(x+3) − 1 < 0, frozen
items.text: Domain from −3, zero at −2: level 1 keeps the crossing just k² = 1 unit from the edge.

items.caption: √(x−1) − 4 < 0, frozen
items.text: Level 4 pushes the zero to 1 + 16 = 17: sixteen units of runway for a square root to climb four.
